US Companies Registering Trademarks in China: A Country Guide

A US registration is a US right. In China it carries no weight, and the mark on your goods is not necessarily the one Chinese consumers use. This guide covers the filing rules from the point of view of a US owner, including the short response windows that catch teams out.

The Local-Agent Rule Comes First

A foreign applicant with no habitual residence or place of business in China must file through a trademark agency lawfully established or registered in China. Article 11 of the 2026 Trademark Law continues the rule. Even a large US company with a China sales team files through the local agent, so appoint one before any deadline is in play.

A branch office in China does not by itself count as a place of business for this purpose, so the exemption does not apply, and there is no special treatment for US applicants. Keep a standing power of attorney on file and keep the applicant name and address consistent. See Who Can Register a Trademark in China for the baseline.

A US Registration Has No Effect in China

China is a first-to-file jurisdiction and a US registration confers no rights there. An English or Latin word mark and a Chinese-character mark are separate rights. Register the official Chinese name, the common transliterations and the nicknames consumers coin themselves; similarity is judged by sound, form and meaning, so a lookalike Chinese-character mark can conflict even where the Latin marks differ. A US owner that filed only the English mark often discovers the Chinese name belongs to someone else.

Decide the official Chinese rendering once, use it on packaging and in filings, and clear the alternatives before launch. This is why a Chinese-character clearance search belongs at the start of market entry rather than after a product is listed. Compare an overseas R mark versus a China registration and logo versus word mark.

See also the first-to-file guide and the Chinese-name case studies.

Priority and the 15/30-Day Madrid Response Windows

Under the Paris Convention, a mark first filed abroad may be filed in China within six months for the same mark and the same goods or services with a priority claim. The claim must be made in writing at filing and a copy of the first application submitted within three months (Article 29 of the 2026 law, corresponding to old Article 25). First use at an international exhibition also carries a six-month priority right.

Those windows are short enough that a US legal team cannot gather instructions after the notice arrives. Pre-authorise the Chinese agent and compare Madrid versus direct filing before choosing a route.

Apostille, Language and Filing Documents

Applications are filed in Chinese. Foreign-language entity certificates need a Chinese translation, and the applicant name and address must correspond in English and Chinese. A power of attorney is generally valid with a signature or seal, so do not assume notarisation or legalisation is always required.

Where public documents do need authentication, the United States is a party to the Hague Apostille Convention, which took effect for China on 7 November 2023. Documents from contracting states use an Apostille instead of the traditional foreign-ministry-plus-embassy double legalisation; non-contracting states still use consular legalisation. Whether the Apostille route applies depends on the document type and what the receiving office currently accepts, so confirm current practice with the agent. Do not assume a fixed fee or processing timeline that is not stated in the official rules.

The 2027 Law and Defensive Portfolios

The 2026 Trademark Law takes effect on 1 January 2027. Article 19 regulates bad-faith applications, including those filed with no intent to use and clearly beyond normal business needs. US owners that built large defensive combinations of marks they never planned to trade under should review those holdings: a purely speculative filing is exactly the pattern the provision targets, and Article 57 separately lets CNIPA cancel a mark unused for three consecutive years on its own initiative.

Article 36 shortens the opposition period from three months to two months, Article 21 extends cross-class protection to unregistered well-known marks, Article 55 addresses licence recordal and statutory termination rights, and Article 46 introduces substantive examination of assignments. The direction is clear: a defensible portfolio is one that is used, watched and documented. See the use-evidence guide and the two-month watch SOP.

Do not assume any special treatment for US applicants, or any official fee, success rate or timeline not stated in the current official rules. Confirm the details with your agent.

Sources and Caveats

Sources: Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision), Articles 11, 19, 21, 29, 36, 46, 55 and 57; the Paris Convention; the Hague Apostille Convention (in force for China from 7 November 2023); WIPO's official Time Limits table for provisional refusals; CNIPA practice on Chinese-language filings. Procedures may be refined by implementing rules, so confirm current official requirements. This is general information, not legal advice.
